The Spanish Empire. The Spanish Empire was a global imperial power spanning the sixteenth through nineteenth centuries. At its height, it was the largest empire in the world by territorial extent, spanning vast regions of the Americas, the Caribbean, much of Europe including the Netherlands and parts of Italy, Africa, and Asia notably the Philippines. Built on the foundations of Columbus's trans-Atlantic voyages and the Reconquista of the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule, the Spanish Empire accumulated vast wealth from American silver and sugar, established Spanish as a global language, and shaped the cultural, religious, and political landscape of the Americas for centuries.

Spain's empire began to coalesce after the marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella in fourteen sixty-nine, which unified the Spanish crowns. Their sponsorship of Columbus in fourteen ninety-two inaugurated Spanish colonization of the Americas and initiated Europe's global expansion. Spanish conquistadors, most notably Hernán Cortés who conquered the Aztec Empire and Francisco Pizarro who conquered the Inca Empire, rapidly subjugated vast populations in the sixteenth century, extracting enormous wealth in gold and silver.

The wealth of the Americas, particularly the silver mines of Potosí in Peru, enriched Spain and financed its wars and court. Spain became the wealthiest power in Europe, though the influx of silver eventually contributed to inflation and economic decline. Spain's American empire relied on the encomienda system, a labor arrangement that granted Spanish settlers control over Indigenous populations. This system, along with disease and warfare, devastated American populations and created a legacy of exploitation and racial stratification.

King Philip II reigned from fifteen fifty-six to fifteen ninety-eight, consolidating imperial power and launching the Spanish Armada against England in fifteen eighty-eight. The Armada's defeat signaled Spain's inability to remain unchallenged at sea and marked the beginning of Spanish decline relative to rising powers like England and the Netherlands. Spain maintained vast territorial claims throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries despite losing ground to other European powers. The Spanish succession crisis between seventeen oh-one and seventeen fourteen further diminished Spanish power and territory in Europe.

The Spanish Empire reached from Mexico and the Caribbean in the north to Chile and Argentina in the south. Spanish colonial administration, Catholic missions, and Spanish language created a lasting cultural unity across these regions. By the nineteenth century, Spanish America had experienced waves of independence movements led by figures like Simón Bolívar. By the end of the century, Spain retained only a few colonial holdings including Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines until the Spanish-American War in eighteen ninety-eight ended most remaining empire.
